Reviewer #3 (Recommendations for the authors):

The authors propose an original dopaminergic learning rule, which, when implemented in simple neural circuit motifs shown to exist within the Drosophila mushroom body (MB) , can potentially account for a very large number of independent, poorly integrated physiological and behavioural phenomena associated with the mushroom body. It considers multiple behavioural roles of MB output neurons beyond attraction and aversion and offers new insight to the how the MB functions in acquisition, consolidation and forgetting of memories. The manuscript further attempts to show how similar principles could potentially be useful in the mammalian brain. An ambitious and integrative analysis of this sort is sorely needed in the field.

The paper has obviously involved very broad and deep consideration of the MB connectome as well as genetic, physiological and behavioural studies of the roles of the different classes of Kenyon cells, MBONs and DANs that innervate the mushroom body. It is original and ambitious and potentially very valuable to the field.

My major reservation is that the manuscript is very difficult to read and evaluate by anyone who is not a Drosophila mushroom body aficionado. I consider myself an interested reader and one who keeps broad track of the field, but found the need to read and evaluate far too many papers cited by the authors to decide how well phenomena the authors attempt to model have been demonstrated and how well assumptions made by the authors are justified by data. E.g. I was stymied even at figure 1, where mutual inhibition between MBONs is indicated and it took me considerable (and eventually futile) effort to look into where and how well this has been established.

To make the work more accessible at least to this moderately educated reviewer, I fear that a major re-rewrite will be required. I would suggest that for each section – exactly has been shown be clearly enumerated, with enough detail provided for the reader to judge the strength of these data. The justification and support for three types of MBONs and their incentive should also be particularly clearly indicated.

Moreover, while the authors are correct to point out the limitations of current models based on dopamine prediction-error, I do wonder if there is room for prediction error to also contribute meaningfully within the framework proposed in this paper.

I apologise for the not having a list of specific issues for the authors to address, because I found the basis to be so difficult to explore but here is some general feedback.

1. It is nice that and the dynamics of neural responses obtained with the model correspond closely with ones reported in previous studies (although there are exceptions, some nicely highlighted by the authors).

2. There should be deeper engagement with signalling mechanisms that differentiate the two types of dopamine receptors. I found the assumptions regarding their differences to be useful for the modelling of different effects of reinforcement before or after sensory experience (Ruta Cell 2019), but quite superficial in terms of providing hypothesis for how the receptors may differ in terms of mechanism of action.

3. ON the same note, specific experimental predictions of the model could also be clearly indicated at the end of each section.

4. While the authors admittedly designed informative and clear figures, and their Table 1 points the reader to papers that report relevant neural connections and neuronal functions, this is not enough. Data in support of each assumption should be clearly and specifically mentioned and hypotheses connections also clearly stated. After considerable effort, I still could find no evidence for lthe existence of inhibitory connections between MBONγ4 and MBONγ2 (which is not to say that none exist – but surely it is the authors job to clarify this).

5. The authors should also try to account for the discovery of parallel, independent memory traces (like appetitive LTM formation towards the CS- in classic LTM aversive training paradigms).

6. Does the dopaminergic learning rule explain the differences in dynamics and memory strength between appetitive and aversive memories? These two types of memory involved different molecular components and display different learning rules (stronger short-term aversive memories and longer-lasting appetitive memories requiring less training)? This should perhaps be clarified, particularly since KC output appears dispensable for aversive learning (aquisition) but potentially necessary for the acquisition of appetitive memories (Pribbenow et al., 2021).

7. I found the easy assumption that forgetting involves erasure to be troubling. Perhaps this happens sometimes. But many apparently "forgotten" memories are never erased, simply not reactivated for multiple reasons. Intellectually this point needs to be acknowledged.

Reviewer #2 (Recommendations for the authors):

The authors propose an original dopaminergic learning rule, which, when implemented in simple neural circuit motifs shown to exist within the Drosophila mushroom body (MB), can potentially account for a very large number of independent, poorly integrated physiological and behavioural phenomena associated with the mushroom body. It considers multiple behavioural roles of MB output neurons beyond attraction and aversion and offers new insight to the how the MB functions in acquisition, consolidation and forgetting of short and long-term memories. They discuss how the motifs and computations discussed would be relevant to other MB functions and altered by known connections, not yet included the simplified model. The manuscript further attempts to show how similar principles could potentially be useful in the mammalian brain. An ambitious and integrative analysis of this sort is sorely needed in the field.

I thank the authors for a very constructive, clear and insightful response to the prior criticism and queries, The manuscript is now hugely improved and can be accepted with no further changes. I think it represents a major contribution to the field. This is a wonderful piece of work that I, at any rate, would recommend to anyone interested in the mushroom body.

Reviewer #3 (Recommendations for the authors):

First, I'd like to thank the authors for responding to my concerns/suggestions. At this point, it reads, in my assessment, much better as a result of the many changes. In particular, the newer figures are of high quality and their stated goals much easier to grasp. Also, shifting most of the discussion of the "formal" model in the (old) Results section to the (new) Methods section makes reading flow more intuitively.

Second, the disagreement we had, appears now to be more in terms of naming/labelling of Equation (18) and (30), thus clarifying the rational for the naming of the 2 learning rules (DPR) and (RPE). However, the "RPE" naming for (30) is, in my view, a bit of a stretch, but I am not raising an objection. Just a friendly note to the authors.

I'd like to make a final suggestion that future readers might benefit from. Reviewer 1 raised this issue already and the authors addressed the question. However, in my view, the presentation starting with "we postulate a mathematical formulation …" just above Equation (32), seems a bit circular. While the authors answered the question, in terms of intuitive modeling (Equation (34)), the presentation thread I am referring to is rather formal. The D's in Equations (32), (33) are not explicitly defined; the equations, when added up are consistent with the Equation above line 854. While Equation (34) provides the intuition of the decomposition of the weights into 2 terms, this decomposition is by no means unique. Having said that, we are then confronted with Equations (35) and (36). There is little justification given for the rational of choosing/postulating these two diff. Equations. I presume that the solution for these Equations are the D's. A careful reading seems to suggest that these are delayed differential equations. In math terms, a single delayed diff. Equation is infinite dimensional, and essentially intractable. The following Equations (37)-(39), while consistent with the discussion above, do not help clarify the matter. Which brings one back to Equations (32), (33). Finally, the Methods section has a sizable number of matrices that have seemingly arbitrary entries.

claims.claim: There are multiple axon terminals of PPL1-γ2α′1 in the mushroom body and each one seems to communicate a different response.

claims.claim: The responses communicated by the MB296B1 terminal are close to the ones produced by the punishment-encoding charging DAN.
claims.source: Interestingly, the responses communicated by the MB296B1 terminal are close to the ones produced by the punishment-encoding charging DAN (see Figure 6C), and the ones of the MB296B2 are close to the ones produced by the attraction-driving forgetting DAN (see Figure 8D).
claims.evidence: This is a comparison of experimental data with model predictions.

claims.claim: Different axons of the same DA neuron might create responses that depend on where the axon terminates and actually work as separate processing units.
claims.source: This implies that different axons of the same DA neuron might create responses that depend on where the axon terminates and actually work as separate processing units.

claims.evidence: This is an inference about the functional consequences of the model mechanism.

claims.source: The depression effect of the forgetting DANs on the KC→restrained MBON synapses of the same valence is supported by Aso et al., 2014a.

claims.evidence: This is based on the connectome data cited from Aso et al., 2014a.

claims.claim: Simulated flies placed in a virtual arena with two odour gradients variously paired with reinforcements allow identification of different aspects of the produced behaviour and motivation.
claims.source: Therefore, we further simulate the behaviour produced by the IC with simulated flies placed in a virtual arena, where they are exposed to two odour gradients, of different strengths, and variously paired with reinforcements. As we have full access to the neural responses, the synaptic weights, and the position of the simulated flies for every time-step, this allows us to identify different aspects of the produced behaviour and motivation, including the effect of the LTM on the behaviour and whether 'choice' occurs because the animal is attracted by one odour or repulsed by the other.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the behavioral simulation approach.

claims.claim: The dopaminergic plasticity rule allows the animal to express a variety of behaviours depending on their experience while remaining very simple.
claims.source: The proposed DPR, while remaining very simple, allows the animal to express a variety of behaviours depending on their experience.
claims.evidence: This is an inference about the properties of the proposed rule.

claims.claim: The dopaminergic plasticity rule remains local to the synapse, depending only on information plausibly available in the presynaptic area of the KC axon.
claims.source: The rule remains local to the synapse, that is, it depends only on information that is plausibly available in the presynaptic area of the KC axon (Equation 1): the activity of the KC, the level of DA, and the deviation of the current 'weight' from a set-point 'resting weight'.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the properties of the proposed rule.

claims.claim: It was not possible to obtain good results without the third component (deviation from resting weight) in the dopaminergic plasticity rule.
claims.source: We note that it was not possible to obtain good results without this third component to the rule, although the underlying biophysical mechanism is unknown; we speculate that it could involve synapsin as it has a direct role in regulating the balance of reserve and release vesicle pools, and is required in the MB for associative learning (Michels et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is an observation from model testing and speculation about the biological mechanism.

claims.claim: The bidirectional dopaminergic factor is based on the results of Handler et al., 2019, who showed the combination of DopR1 and DopR2 receptor activity can result in depression or potentiation of the synapse.
claims.source: The rule also introduces a bidirectional 'dopaminergic factor' based on the results of Handler et al., 2019, who showed the combination of DopR1 and DopR2 receptor activity can result in depression or potentiation of the synapse.
claims.evidence: This is based on cited experimental work.

claims.claim: The saturation effect allows LTM MBONs to consolidate their memories and makes it very hard to forget.
claims.source: In particular, the saturation allows LTM MBONs to consolidate their memories and makes it very hard to forget.
claims.evidence: This is an inference about the functional consequences of the saturation effect.

claims.claim: Only a persistent change in the valence of reinforcement experienced with a given stimuli can reset the activity of LTM MBONs through the reciprocal LTMs microcircuit.
claims.source: This only occurs for consistently experienced associations, which then become strongly embedded. Only a persistent change in the valence of reinforcement experienced with a given stimuli can reset the activity of LTM MBONs through the reciprocal LTMs microcircuit, which equips the circuit with flexibility even in the LTMs.
claims.evidence: This is an inference about the functional consequences of the model mechanism.

claims.claim: The memory assimilation mechanism increases the capacity of the circuit by allowing restrained MBON learning to be eventually assimilated by the LTM MBONs.
claims.source: Further, the fact that the DPR allows STMs (restrained) and LTMs to interact through the memory assimilation mechanism (MAM) increases the capacity of the circuit. Whatever the restrained MBONs learn is eventually assimilated by the LTM MBONs, opening up space for the formation of new memories in the restrained MBONs.
claims.evidence: This is an inference about the functional consequences of the model mechanism.

claims.claim: When combined with sparse coding of odours in a large number of KCs, the LTM MBONs can store multiple memories for different odours.
claims.source: When combined with sparse coding of odours in a large number of KCs, the LTM MBONs can store multiple memories for different odours.
claims.evidence: This is an inference about the functional consequences of the model mechanism.

claims.claim: The reward prediction error plasticity rule lacks the flexibility of the dopaminergic plasticity rule and fails to maintain useful LTMs when applied to the same circuit architecture.
claims.source: By contrast, the RPE plasticity rule lacks this flexibility and fails to maintain useful LTMs when applied to the same circuit architecture.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing model results with RPE vs DPR.

claims.claim: A literal interpretation of RPE for the mushroom body would require that the difference between the postsynaptic MBON activity and the DA level is calculated in the presynaptic KC axon.
claims.source: A literal interpretation of RPE for the MB would require that the difference (error) between the postsynaptic MBON activity and the DA level is somehow calculated in the presynaptic KC axon.
claims.evidence: This is an inference about the requirements of RPE implementation.

claims.claim: The literal interpretation of RPE seems inconsistent with the observation that learning is generally unaffected by silencing the MBONs during acquisition.
claims.source: This seems inconsistent with the observation that learning is generally unaffected by silencing the MBONs during acquisition (Hige et al., 2015; Krashes et al., 2007; Dubnau et al., 2001; McGuire et al., 2001).
claims.evidence: This is based on cited experimental observations.

claims.claim: The evidence for MBON-DAN feedback connections is well-grounded, but it is less clear that they are consistently opposing.
claims.source: However, although the evidence for MBON-DAN feedback connections is well-grounded, it is less clear that they are consistently opposing.
claims.evidence: This is an assessment of the evidence from the literature.

claims.claim: Some DANs that depress synaptic weights receive inhibitory feedback from MBONs.
claims.source: For example, in the microcircuits we have described, based on neurophysiological evidence, some DANs that depress synaptic weights receive inhibitory feedback from MBONs (Pavlowsky et al., 2018) and some DANs that potentiate synaptic weights receive excitatory feedback from DANs (Ichinose et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is based on cited experimental work.

claims.claim: The dopaminergic plasticity rule is able to operate with a variety of MBON-DAN connections.
claims.source: As we have shown, the DPR is able to operate with this variety of MBON-DAN connections.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the model results.

claims.claim: By using the appropriate circuit with positive MBON-DAN feedback to depressing DANs, the dopaminergic plasticity rule could also have a reward prediction error effect.
claims.source: Note that, by using the appropriate circuit, that is, positive MBON-DAN feedback to depressing DANs, our DPR could also have an RPE effect.
claims.evidence: This is speculation about the potential of the proposed rule.

claims.claim: The model supports backward (relief) conditioning results presented in Handler et al., 2019.
claims.source: In the methods section 'Derivation of the dopaminergic plasticity rule', we demonstrate that our model supports the backward (or relief) conditioning results presented in Handler et al., 2019.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated in the methods section.

claims.claim: Handler et al., 2019 suggest that backward conditioning is a mechanism driven by ER-Ca2+ and cAMP in a KC→MBON synapse when a single DAN releases DA on it.
claims.source: Handler et al., 2019 suggest that the backward conditioning is a mechanism driven by ER-Ca2+ and cAMP in a KC→MBON synapse, when a single DAN releases DA on it.
claims.evidence: This is a citation to previous experimental work.

claims.claim: In the model, different time courses in the response of DopR1 and DopR2 receptors cause the different patterns of ER-Ca2+ and cAMP, resulting in opposite associations for forward and backward conditioning.
claims.source: In our model, we assume that different time courses in the response of DopR1 and DopR2 receptors cause the different patterns of ER-Ca2+ and cAMP, resulting in the formation of opposite associations for forward and backward conditioning.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the model mechanism.

claims.claim: The backward conditioning effect in the model requires that the target MBON inhibits the respective DAN, altering the time course of neurotransmitter release.
claims.source: We note however that in our model the effect also requires that the target MBON inhibits the respective DAN (as in our susceptible memory microcircuits) altering the time course of neurotransmitter release.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the model mechanism.

claims.claim: Backward conditioning may not occur in all mushroom body compartments.
claims.source: This may suggest that backward conditioning does not occur in all MB compartments.
claims.evidence: This is speculation based on the model mechanism.

claims.claim: The mechanism for backward conditioning in the model is better supported than the hypothesised mechanism of post-inhibitory rebound in opposing valence DANs presented in Adel and Griffith, 2021.
claims.source: We believe that this mechanism for backward conditioning is better supported than the hypothesised mechanism of post-inhibitory rebound in opposing valence DANs presented in Adel and Griffith, 2021, although some role for both mechanisms is possible.
claims.evidence: This is a comparison with an alternative hypothesis from the literature.

claims.claim: Unpaired conditioning involves the presentation of reinforcement and a specific odour in alternation with less temporal proximity.
claims.source: Backward conditioning can be distinguished from the unpaired conditioning effect; the latter involves the presentation of reinforcement and a specific odour in alternation with less temporal proximity.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about conditioning paradigms.

claims.claim: Unpaired conditioning produces a change in response to the odour that is opposite in valence to the reinforcement.
claims.source: It has been observed (Jacob and Waddell, 2020; Schleyer et al., 2018) that this procedure will produce a change in response to the odour that is opposite in valence to the reinforcement, for example, approach to an odour that is 'unpaired' with shock.
claims.evidence: This is based on cited experimental observations.

claims.claim: The model produces unpaired conditioning through a different mechanism than backward conditioning.
claims.source: Surprisingly, our model also produces unpaired conditioning, notably through a different mechanism than backward conditioning.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the model results.

claims.claim: When DANs are activated by a reinforcement without KC activation, the weights of all KCs are potentially altered.
claims.source: When DANs are activated by a reinforcement without KC activation, the weights of all KCs are potentially altered, for example, restored towards their resting weight or slightly potentiated.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the model mechanism.

claims.claim: Subsequent presentation of odour alone can be accompanied by MBON-driven activation of DANs, resulting in specific alteration of the weights for the presented odour.
claims.source: This alteration means that subsequent presentation of odour alone can be accompanied by MBON-driven activation of DANs, resulting in specific alteration of the weights for the presented odour.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the model mechanism.

claims.claim: In the unpaired conditioning example, odour A starts to self-reinforce its attractive LTM when presented in alternation with shock and will be preferred to an alternative odour B in subsequent testing.
claims.source: In the example of Figure 12, odour A starts to self-reinforce its attractive LTM when presented in alternation with shock and will be preferred to an alternative odour B in subsequent testing.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated in the model results shown in Figure 12.

claims.claim: Repeated presentation of other odours during testing without further shock might lead to generalisation (equal preference to all experienced odours).
claims.source: However, repeated presentation of other odours during testing, without further shock, might lead to generalisation (equal preference to all experienced odours).
claims.evidence: This is a prediction from the model mechanism.

claims.claim: The self-reinforcing property of the positive feedback in the LTM microcircuit can account for second-order conditioning.
claims.source: The self-reinforcing property of the positive feedback in the LTM microcircuit can also account for second-order conditioning.
claims.evidence: This is an inference about the functional consequences of the model mechanism.

claims.claim: If a motivation has been associated to an odour, MBONs related to that motivation will have increased activity when the odour is delivered, even in the absence of reinforcement.
claims.source: If a motivation has been associated to an odour, MBONs related to that motivation will have increased activity when the odour is delivered, even in the absence of reinforcement.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the model mechanism.

claims.claim: In the LTM microcircuit, the positive MBON-DAN connection will activate the charging DAN when a learned odour is presented, so any additional cue presented alongside will also experience an increase in the respective KC→MBON weights.
claims.source: In the LTM microcircuit, the positive MBON-DAN connection will consequently activate the charging DAN, so any additional cue (or KC activity) presented alongside the learned odour will also experience an increase in the respective KC→MBON weights, creating a similar charging momentum and resulting in a second-order association.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the model mechanism.

claims.claim: Second-order conditioning might happen directly in the LTM microcircuit without being filtered by the susceptible and restrained memories first.
claims.source: Perhaps surprisingly, this predicts that second-order conditioning might happen directly in the LTM microcircuit without being filtered by the susceptible and restrained memories first.
claims.evidence: This is a prediction from the model mechanism.

claims.claim: The prediction that second-order conditioning occurs directly in LTM would be consistent with the observation that second-order conditioning in flies requires strong induction of the first-order memory and that first-order memory does not appear to be extinguished by the absence of reinforcement during second-order training.
claims.source: This would be consistent with the observation that second-order conditioning in flies requires strong induction of the first-order memory and that first-order memory does not appear to be extinguished by the absence of reinforcement during second-order training (Tabone and de Belle, 2011).
claims.evidence: This is a comparison of model predictions with experimental observations.

claims.claim: The dopaminergic plasticity rule would not produce blocking.
claims.source: Finally, although we have not tested it explicitly here, it is clear that our plasticity rule (unlike RPE) would not produce blocking.
claims.evidence: This is an inference about the properties of the proposed rule.

claims.claim: The blocking effect is when the conditioning to one stimulus subsequently blocks any conditioning to other elements of a mixture including that stimulus.
claims.source: The blocking effect, as described by Kamin, 1967, is when the conditioning to one stimulus subsequently blocks any conditioning to other elements of a mixture including that stimulus.
claims.evidence: This is a citation to established psychological theory.

claims.claim: Under RPE learning, blocking is explained by the first stimulus already correctly predicting the reinforcer, so there is no error to drive a change in the weights.
claims.source: Under RPE learning, this is explained by the first stimulus already correctly predicting the reinforcer, so there is no error to drive a change in the weights.
claims.evidence: This is an explanation of RPE theory.

claims.claim: Using the dopaminergic plasticity rule, the updates are local to the synapse and do not depend on a calculation of errors summarised across different odour identities, so blocking does not happen.
claims.source: Using the DPR, the updates are local to the synapse and do not depend on a calculation of errors summarised across different odour identities, so blocking does not happen, which is consistent with the observed behaviour of fruit flies (Young et al., 2011; Brembs and Heisenberg, 2001).
claims.evidence: This is an inference about the properties of the proposed rule compared with experimental observations.

claims.claim: The model suggests that only KC→MBON, MBON⊣DAN, MBON→DAN, and DAN⊸MBON connections are essential for successful learning in the mushroom bodies.
claims.source: Our model suggests that only KC→MBON, MBON⊣DAN, MBON→DAN, and DAN⊸MBON connections are essential for successful learning in the MBs.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the model results.

claims.claim: There are additional known connections in the mushroom bodies, such as KC→APL, APL⊣KC, DAN→MBON, axoaxonic KC→KC and KC→DAN connections that have been neglected in this model.
claims.source: However, there are a number of additional known connections in the MBs, such as KC→APL, APL⊣KC, DAN→MBON, axoaxonic KC→KC and KC→DAN connections that have been neglected in this model, and need further consideration.
claims.evidence: This is an acknowledgment of limitations of the model.

claims.claim: In the larval brain, there are two anterior paired lateral (APL) neurons, one for each mushroom body.
claims.source: In the larval brain, there are two anterior paired lateral (APL) neurons, one for each MB.
claims.evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge.

claims.claim: APL neurons extend their dendrites to the lobes of the mushroom bodies and terminate their axons in the calyxes releasing the inhibitory GABA neurotransmitter.
claims.source: They extend their dendrites to the lobes of the MBs and terminate their axons in the calyxes releasing the inhibitory GABA neurotransmitter (Tanaka et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This is based on cited anatomical studies.

claims.claim: In the adult brain, both APL dendrites and axons innervate the calyx and the lobes, suggesting they function as both global and local inhibitory circuits.
claims.source: Although there are still two of them, in the adult brain both their dendrites and axons are innervating the calyx and the lobes (Wu et al., 2013), suggesting that they function as both global and local inhibitory circuits.
claims.evidence: This is based on cited anatomical studies and inference about function.

claims.claim: DAN⊣APL and APL⊣DAN connections have been proposed, but there is no clear description of what their function is.
claims.source: Moreover, DAN⊣APL (Liu and Davis, 2009) and APL⊣DAN (Wu et al., 2012) connections have been proposed, but there is no clear description of what their function is.
claims.evidence: This is based on cited studies and an assessment of the literature.

claims.claim: A potential function for the global/local inhibition network involving APL is gain control such that the total number of KCs firing to different stimuli remains similar.
claims.source: Several previous models (Peng and Chittka, 2017; Delahunt et al., 2018) have demonstrated that a potential function for this global/local inhibition network is gain control such that the total number of KCs firing to different stimuli remains similar, and indeed that the same effect can be implemented using a flexible threshold for KC firing (Saumweber et al., 2018; Zhu et al., 2020; Zhao et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is based on cited modeling studies.

claims.claim: The model simplified the KC input, representing just two odours as different patterns across a small number of KCs with a fixed number of them being active at all times, so the hypothesised gain control function of the APL is not useful.
claims.source: In our model, we have simplified the KC input, representing just two odours as different patterns across a small number of KCs with a fixed number of them being active at all times, so the hypothesised gain control function of the APL is not useful here.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the model simplification.

claims.claim: It remains an interesting question whether there is learning between the KC and APL in the lobes, or between the APL and KC in the calyx, and what role this might play in the overall dynamics of memory acquisition.
claims.source: However, it remains an interesting question whether there is learning between the KC and APL in the lobes (Zhou et al., 2019), or between the APL and KC in the calyx, and what role this might play in the overall dynamics of memory acquisition.
claims.evidence: This is speculation about potential mechanisms not included in the model.

claims.claim: Eichler et al., 2017 suggest that most of the KCs input (60%) is from other KCs.
claims.source: In addition, Eichler et al., 2017 suggest that most of the KCs input, that is, 60%, is from other KCs.
claims.evidence: This is a citation to previous anatomical work.

claims.claim: KC-KC connections together with APL connections might create local winner-takes-all networks that force a limited number of KCs per compartment to be active at one time.
claims.source: We suggest that these connections (together with the ones from the APL) might create local winner-takes-all (WTA) networks that force a limited number of KCs per compartment to be active at one time.
claims.evidence: This is speculation about the function of these connections.

claims.claim: It is possible for the same KC axon to be active in one compartment but inactive in another.
claims.source: This predicts that it is possible for the same KC axon to be active in one compartment but inactive in another (consistent with recent data from Bilz et al., 2020), and that an almost fixed number of KCs might be active at all times, even when no odour is delivered (e.g., fresh air only) enabling the acquisition and forgetting at all times.
claims.evidence: This is a prediction from the proposed mechanism that is consistent with cited data.

claims.claim: Ito et al., 2008 show that KCs can be active even in the absence of odours but with no consistent spiking, which is a characteristic of winner-takes-all networks when the underlying distribution of spikes across the neurons is almost uniform.
claims.source: Ito et al., 2008 show that KCs can be active even in the absence of odours but with no consistent spiking, which is a characteristic of WTA networks when the underlying distribution of spikes across the neurons is almost uniform.
claims.evidence: This is a citation to experimental observations and an inference about their interpretation.

claims.claim: Eichler et al., 2017 observed that within a compartment, in a 'canonical microcircuit', KCs make direct synapses to the axons of DANs, and that DAN pre-synapses often simultaneously contact KCs and MBONs.
claims.source: Eichler et al., 2017 also observed (from electron microscopy reconstruction in larva) that within a compartment, in a 'canonical microcircuit', KCs make direct synapses to the axons of DANs, and that DAN pre-synapses often simultaneously contact KCs and MBONs.
claims.evidence: This is a citation to anatomical observations.

claims.claim: The same KC→DAN and DAN→KC/MBON connections observed in larva have been observed in adult Drosophila by Takemura et al., 2017.
claims.source: The same connections have been observed in adult Drosophila by Takemura et al., 2017.
claims.evidence: This is a citation to anatomical observations.

claims.claim: The extent to which KCs might be directly exciting DANs remains unclear.
claims.source: The extent to which KCs (and thus odour inputs) might be directly exciting DANs remains unclear.

claims.claim: Cervantes-Sandoval et al., 2017 show that stimulating KCs results in increased DAN responses and that DANs are activated through the ACh neurotransmitter.

results.result: The authors propose a novel dopaminergic plasticity rule (DPR) that depends on KC activity, dopamine level, and deviation from resting weight, producing four effects (depression, potentiation, recovery, saturation) that maximize separation between synaptic weights of reinforced inputs.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C22-C23, C25, C27-C28, C97-C100 collectively describe the DPR and its properties. The rule is mathematically defined (Equation 1), illustrated in Figure 2, and shown to be necessary for model function (C99). The four effects are derived from the mathematical formulation and demonstrated in simulations. The rule's locality and biological plausibility are discussed with appropriate caveats about unknown mechanisms.

results.result: The incentive circuit consists of six MBONs (susceptible, restrained, LTM for each of attraction/avoidance) and six DANs (discharging, charging, forgetting for each valence) with specific connectivity patterns that enable memory dynamics.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C40, C160 describe the structure and basic function of the proposed incentive circuit. The circuit is illustrated in Figure 3, connectivity is mapped to identified neurons in Table 1, and the functional roles of each neuron type are clearly defined. The circuit structure is derived from published connectome data with appropriate citations.

results.result: The susceptible memory microcircuit, consisting of PPL1-γ1pedc (punishment DAN), MBON-γ1pedc>α/β (attraction MBON), and MBON-γ5β'2a (avoidance MBON), produces rapid memory acquisition with high learning rate and low retention time, matching experimental observations.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C54 describe the susceptible memory circuit and compare model predictions with experimental data. Figure 5 shows good qualitative agreement between model and experimental neural responses during conditioning. The rapid learning (C46) and recovery effects (C48-C49) are demonstrated. The positive feedback mechanism (C53) is clearly explained and contrasted with RPE (C54).

results.result: A mirror susceptible/restrained memory circuit with opposite valence exists, with proposed identities PAM-γ4<γ1γ2 (reward DAN), MBON-γ4>γ1γ2 (avoidance MBON), and MBON-γ2α'1 (attraction MBON).
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C61 propose a symmetric circuit based on connectome analysis (C55). However, the specific neuron identifications (C57-C59) are inferences from the model rather than direct experimental validation. The mechanism for inhibitory glutamate signaling (C61) is speculative. While anatomically plausible, this circuit lacks the direct experimental validation shown for the aversive circuit.

results.result: The reciprocal short-term memories microcircuit, where restrained MBONs activate charging DANs that depress opposite-valence restrained MBONs, maintains balance between memories and produces fragile short-term memories.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C68 describe the reciprocal STM circuit with support from multiple citations (C62-C64). The circuit structure is shown in Figure 6, and the functional consequences (C66-C67) are demonstrated in simulations. The prediction that these store STMs (C68) follows logically from the demonstrated fragility. The circuit is grounded in published connectivity data.

results.result: The long-term memory microcircuit features positive feedback between LTM MBONs and charging DANs, enabling memory consolidation through the saturation effect even after reinforcement ceases.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C77 describe the LTM circuit and its self-reinforcing properties. The circuit is based on published connectivity (C69-C70) and illustrated in Figure 7. The positive feedback mechanism (C73) and saturation effect (C74) are clearly explained. The model demonstrates continued memory strengthening (C75), though experimental data don't show this clearly (C76), which is reasonably explained by individual experience variability (C77).

results.result: The reciprocal long-term memories microcircuit uses forgetting DANs activated by LTM MBONs to depress opposite-valence LTM, enabling long-term competition and flexibility. Different axon terminals of PPL1-γ2α'1 may function as separate processing units.
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C89 describe the reciprocal LTM mechanism. The circuit structure (C79-C81) and functional consequences (C82-C83) are clearly explained. The mapping to identified neurons (C84) is based on published connectome data. The observation about multiple axon terminals (C86-C88) is supported by experimental data (Figure 4—supplement 1), and model predictions match observed responses surprisingly well (C89, Figure 8C-D).

results.result: The memory assimilation mechanism, where forgetting DANs also suppress restrained MBON synapses of the same valence, enables memory transfer from short-term to long-term storage.
results.evaluation: Claims C90-C94 describe the MAM circuit. The prediction (C90) is illustrated in Figure 9C, and the functional consequence (C91) is demonstrated in simulations. The anatomical support (C92-C94) is based on published connectome data from Aso et al., 2014a. The mechanism provides a plausible explanation for STM-to-LTM transfer observed behaviorally.

results.result: The complete incentive circuit model enables rapid memory acquisition, STM-to-LTM transfer, exploration/exploitation trade-off, reproduces observed neural responses during conditioning, and enables flexible behavioral control.
results.evaluation: Claims C4-C8, C96 describe the integrated capabilities of the full model. Rapid acquisition is demonstrated in Figure 5, STM-to-LTM transfer through the MAM (Figure 9), neural response reproduction throughout Figures 5-8, and behavioral control in Figures 10-11. The model correlates well with 92 intervention experiments (r=0.76, Figure 3—supplement 1) and produces realistic behavior in virtual arena simulations.

results.result: The saturation effect enables LTM consolidation resistant to forgetting, with flexibility only through persistent opposite-valence reinforcement. The memory assimilation mechanism increases circuit capacity by transferring restrained MBON learning to LTM MBONs.
results.evaluation: Claims C101-C104 describe functional advantages of the DPR and circuit architecture. The saturation effect's role in LTM consolidation (C101) is demonstrated in simulations. The requirement for persistent opposite reinforcement (C102) follows from the reciprocal LTM circuit dynamics. The capacity increase through MAM (C103) and ability to store multiple odor memories (C104) are demonstrated in behavioral simulations (Figure 11).

results.result: The reward prediction error plasticity rule lacks the flexibility of DPR, fails to maintain useful LTMs in the same circuit, and requires implausible mechanisms inconsistent with experimental observations of learning during MBON silencing.
results.evaluation: Claims C105-C111 compare DPR with RPE. The failure of RPE in the same circuit (C105) is demonstrated in Figure 9—supplements 2-3 and Figure 11—supplements 5-7. The implausibility of literal RPE implementation (C106-C107) is supported by citations to experiments showing learning without MBON activity. The assessment of MBON-DAN feedback evidence (C108-C109) is reasonable, and DPR's flexibility (C110) is demonstrated throughout the results.

results.result: The model supports backward conditioning through differential time courses of DopR1 and DopR2 responses, requiring MBON inhibition of the DAN, suggesting backward conditioning may not occur in all MB compartments.
results.evaluation: Claims C112-C117 describe backward conditioning in the model. The support for Handler et al. 2019 results (C112) is demonstrated in Figure 16 with good quantitative agreement (r=0.98). The mechanism (C113-C114) is clearly explained with mathematical detail in the methods. The requirement for MBON-DAN inhibition (C115) and prediction about compartment specificity (C116) are logical inferences. The comparison with alternative mechanisms (C117) is reasonable.

results.result: The model produces unpaired conditioning through a different mechanism than backward conditioning: reinforcement without KC activation alters all KC weights, then odor presentation with MBON-driven DAN activation specifically alters weights for that odor.
results.evaluation: Claims C118-C124 describe unpaired conditioning. The distinction from backward conditioning (C118) is clear. The mechanism (C120-C122) is explained and differs from backward conditioning. The demonstration in Figure 12 (C123) shows the predicted effect. The prediction about generalization (C124) is a reasonable inference from the mechanism. This emergent property of the model is consistent with experimental observations (C119).

results.result: The positive feedback in the LTM microcircuit can account for second-order conditioning, potentially occurring directly in LTM without filtering through susceptible and restrained memories, consistent with observations that second-order conditioning requires strong first-order memory.
results.evaluation: Claims C125-C129 describe second-order conditioning. The mechanism (C125-C127) follows logically from the LTM circuit structure. The prediction about direct LTM involvement (C128) is a novel inference from the model. The consistency with experimental observations (C129) provides support, though direct experimental validation of the proposed mechanism is not provided. This is a reasonable prediction requiring future testing.

results.result: The DPR would not produce blocking because updates are local to the synapse and do not depend on error calculations across odor identities, consistent with observed fruit fly behavior.
results.evaluation: Claims C130-C133 address blocking. The prediction that DPR doesn't produce blocking (C130) follows logically from the rule's local nature. The explanation of blocking under RPE (C131-C132) is accurate. The consistency with fly behavior (C133) is supported by appropriate citations. This is a clear prediction distinguishing DPR from RPE, though not directly tested in the presented experiments.

results.result: The model suggests only KC→MBON, MBON⊣DAN, MBON→DAN, and DAN⊸MBON connections are essential, while additional known connections (KC→APL, APL⊣KC, etc.) are acknowledged but not included, with discussion of their potential roles.
results.evaluation: Claims C134-C142 discuss model limitations and additional connections. The claim about essential connections (C134) is supported by the model's success. The acknowledgment of omitted connections (C135-C139) is appropriate. The discussion of APL function (C140-C141) cites relevant literature. The speculation about learning in KC-APL connections (C142) is appropriately tentative. This represents honest assessment of model scope and limitations.

results.result: KC-KC connections might create local winner-takes-all networks forcing limited KC activity per compartment, predicting compartment-specific KC activity and enabling continuous acquisition/forgetting.
results.evaluation: Claims C143-C146 propose a role for KC-KC connections. The anatomical observation (C143) is cited. The WTA hypothesis (C144) is speculation. The predictions (C145-C146) are supported by some cited data (Bilz et al. 2020, Ito et al. 2008) but the proposed mechanism is not tested. This is reasonable speculation requiring experimental validation.

results.result: Direct KC→DAN connections exist anatomically but their functional role remains unclear; the model can explain observed DAN responses to odors without requiring direct KC→DAN connections, though they may enhance specificity or provide alternative RPE implementation.
results.evaluation: Claims C147-C156 discuss KC→DAN connections. The anatomical observations (C147-C148) are well-cited. The unclear functional role (C149) is honestly stated. The experimental observations (C150) and alternative model explanation (C151-C153) are clearly presented. The claim that the model explains DAN responses without direct connections (C154) is supported by results. The speculation about potential roles (C155-C156) is appropriately tentative.

results.result: Direct DAN→MBON synapses are functional and could coordinate learned responses with current reinforcement presence, or involve postsynaptic changes in learning.
results.evaluation: Claims C157-C159 discuss DAN→MBON connections. The functional demonstration (C157) is cited. However, the proposed functions (C158-C159) are speculative, based on cited work but not tested in the current model. These represent reasonable hypotheses about mechanisms not included in the current model.

results.result: The incentive circuit motif could be repeated for additional opposing motivations beyond attraction/avoidance, with neurons having multiple context-dependent roles, potentially connecting to ~8 available motivations through γ-KCs.
results.evaluation: Claims C160-C166 propose extensions of the model. The observation about total neuron numbers (C161) is factual. The proposals about repeated motifs (C162), multiple roles (C163), and connections to multiple motivations (C166) are speculative extensions supported by some cited work (Cohn et al. 2015) but not tested. These represent interesting hypotheses for future work rather than demonstrated results.

results.result: Functional analogies are proposed between MB incentive circuit components and mammalian limbic system structures, with susceptible MBONs analogous to amygdala, restrained/LTM MBONs to hypothalamus, and α/β MBONs to cingulate cortex.
results.evaluation: Claims C167-C179 propose functional analogies between insect and mammalian systems. The descriptions of limbic system structure (C168-C172) are based on established literature. However, the proposed mappings (C173-C179) are entirely speculative, based on functional similarities rather than homology or direct evidence. While intellectually interesting, these analogies are not tested and represent speculation about convergent evolution of memory systems.

results.result: Background on insect learning and Drosophila mushroom body anatomy, including established knowledge about KC-MBON-DAN connectivity and their roles in associative learning.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C9-C21 provide background information. These are well-established facts about insect behavior and Drosophila neuroanatomy, appropriately cited to previous literature. This background is necessary context for the novel work but does not constitute a result of the current study.
